content: The recommendations outlined apply to both household and close contacts of tuberculosis (TB) patients. Contact investigation is essential when the TB patient has any of the following characteristics: bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB, suspected or confirmed multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) or extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), is living with HIV, or is a child under the age of five. Screening of contacts can be conducted either at the household of the TB patient or in a clinical setting. However, it is strongly recommended to conduct screening within the household whenever possible. Given the high risk of disease in this group, the most accurate screening and diagnostic algorithms should be employed. Continued monitoring is critical for program managers to evaluate the performance of TB screening interventions. Standard monitoring and evaluation procedures can be supplemented with operational research to improve the effectiveness of screening in local settings and to strengthen the global evidence base on screening. Further research is needed to guide the implementation of contact screening, including strategies to maximize the reach and effectiveness of interventions. This includes ensuring that contacts who screen positive access health facilities for further diagnostic evaluation and initiating preventive treatment for those in whom TB disease is ruled out. Additional research is also required to evaluate the accuracy and effectiveness of comprehensive screening and diagnostic algorithms, including symptom screening, chest X-rays (CXR), and molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) in various combinations. In prison settings, systematic screening for TB disease is recommended over passive case detection. People in prisons, including inmates and staff, are at significantly higher risk of TB compared to the general population. The estimated incidence of TB among prisoners is 23 times higher than in the general population. Observational data from 2010–2020 indicate that screening interventions in prisons can improve early case detection, increase overall TB case detection, and reduce TB prevalence. However, the certainty of evidence remains very low. Screening in prisons should include symptom-based screening, CXR, and mWRDs, depending on the setting and resources available. Studies have shown that symptom-based screening has a mean number needed to screen (NNS) of 248, while CXR-based screening has a mean NNS of 401. The use of mWRDs as a screening strategy has demonstrated a much lower mean NNS of 27 in moderateto medium-burden settings. The implementation of TB screening in prisons should be accompanied by efforts to improve living conditions, infection control, and access to healthcare services. Screening should be conducted at entry, annually, and upon exit from detention facilities to prevent the reintroduction of TB into the broader community. The cost of prison screening programs varies depending on the screening algorithm used. For example, mobile CXR units in Belgium cost €113,325 to screen 7,901 prisoners, while a program in South Africa screening 20,700 inmates cost $730,000. The cost-effectiveness of screening depends on the reduction in TB transmission and the prevention of future cases. While evidence suggests that screening may be cost-effective, further research is needed to confirm this. Screening in prisons is likely to increase health equity by improving access to healthcare services for a population that often has limited access. The use of chest X-rays with computer-aided detection (CAD) software for TB screening, compared to human interpretation, is also being evaluated. CAD software has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of TB screening, particularly in resource-limited settings. In conclusion, systematic TB screening in prisons is strongly recommended due to the high risk of TB in this population and the potential to improve early case detection, reduce TB prevalence, and increase equity in healthcare access. Further research is needed to optimize screening strategies, evaluate cost-effectiveness, and address implementation challenges.
